title: Representability of a finite fibre functor on a category generated by one object
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $\mathcal C$ an essentially small $k$-linear abelian category [def-sp-abelian], meaning that its isomorphism classes form a set, its Hom sets are $k$-vector spaces and composition is bilinear. Let $F:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}}_k$ be an exact faithful $k$-linear functor (it preserves short exact sequences and its maps on Hom spaces are injective and $k$-linear); finite-dimensional means possessing a finite spanning set [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Suppose there is $X\in\mathcal C$ such that every object of $\mathcal C$ is isomorphic to a quotient of a subobject of $X^{\oplus n}$ for some integer $n\geq0$. Then there are $P\in\mathcal C$ and $p\in F(P)$ for which, for every $Y\in\mathcal C$, the map
$$\alpha_Y:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(P,Y)\longrightarrow F(Y),\qquad h\longmapsto F(h)p$$
is a $k$-linear isomorphism, natural in $Y$. They can be chosen with $\dim_kF(P)\leq(\dim_kF(X))^2$. The zero category and $X=0$ are allowed.

source.place: Lemmas 9.33 and 9.34(a), printed pp.175–176: monogenic dimension bound and maximal monogenic representing pair.

proof.text: The exactness result [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology] applies because $F$ is additive by $k$-linearity and preserves short exact sequences. Hence $F$ preserves kernels, cokernels, images and finite biproducts. We will also use that $F$ reflects isomorphisms. Indeed, if $F(u)$ is invertible, faithfulness and cancellation show that $u$ is both mono and epi. By [def-sp-abelian], a monomorphism $u:A\to B$ is a kernel of some $v:B\to C$. Since $vu=0$ and $u$ is epi, $v=0$. The kernel property applied to $1_B$ gives $s:B\to A$ with $us=1_B$; cancellation by $u$ then gives $su=1_A$. Thus $u$ is invertible. This also covers maps between zero objects.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175, paragraph after Theorem 9.32: reflection of zero objects and isomorphisms.

proof.text: For any $V$ and $v\in F(V)$ use [lem-sfb-fibre-generated-subobject] with $S=\{v\}$, and call the resulting subobject $\langle v\rangle\hookrightarrow V$. Write its unique lifted vector as $\widetilde v$; uniqueness uses injectivity of $F$ on monomorphisms from step 1. The pair $(\langle v\rangle,\widetilde v)$ is monogenic: if a subobject $T\hookrightarrow\langle v\rangle$ contains $\widetilde v$ in its fibre, its composite into $V$ contains $v$, so leastness gives a factorization of $\langle v\rangle\hookrightarrow V$ through $T$; cancellation makes $T\hookrightarrow\langle v\rangle$ invertible. Here “$(Y,y)$ is monogenic” means that every subobject of $Y$ whose fibre contains $y$ is the whole of $Y$.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175, last two paragraphs: generated subobject and monogenic object.

proof.text: Put $d=\dim_kF(X)$. Let $(Y,y)$ be monogenic. By the hypothesis choose an epimorphism $e:Y_1\twoheadrightarrow Y$ and a monomorphism $b:Y_1\hookrightarrow X^{\oplus m}$. The map $F(e)$ is onto by [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology], so choose $y_1$ mapping to $y$. Generate $Z=\langle y_1\rangle\subseteq Y_1$ by [lem-sfb-fibre-generated-subobject]. Its lifted generator $z$ makes $Z$ monogenic by step 2. Factor $e|_Z$ through its image $I\hookrightarrow Y$. Preservation of this image shows that $y$ belongs to $F(I)$; monogenicity gives $I=Y$. Consequently $Z\twoheadrightarrow Y$ is onto after $F$, so $\dim F(Y)\leq\dim F(Z)$. We have reduced the bound to a monogenic object $Z$ embedded in a finite sum of copies of $X$, without assuming that a quotient generator already lifts to a generator of $Y_1$.

For a monogenic pair $(Z,z)$ embedded by $b$ in $X^{\oplus m}$, suppose $m>d$. Write $F(b)z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ in $F(X)^m$. There is a nonzero relation $\sum a_i z_i=0$; choose $j$ with $a_j\ne0$. Define $t=\sum a_i\pi_i:X^{\oplus m}\to X$. The kernel of $tb$ contains $z$ in its fibre by [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology]. Monogenicity therefore makes that kernel all of $Z$, so $tb=0$ and $b$ factors monomorphically through $\ker t$. Projection away from coordinate $j$ identifies $\ker t$ with $X^{\oplus(m-1)}$: its inverse inserts coordinate $-a_j^{-1}\sum_{i\ne j}a_i x_i$. These are actual morphisms formed from sums, scalar multiples and biproduct projections and injections; the displayed relation verifies both composites are identities. Induct on $m$: if $m\leq d$ stop; otherwise this construction decreases $m$ by one, with the same $(Z,z)$ and a new embedding. Thus $Z\hookrightarrow X^{\oplus r}$ for $r\leq d$. Its fibre has dimension at most $rd\leq d^2$. Step 3 now gives $\dim F(Y)\leq d^2$ for every monogenic pair. The argument includes $d=0$ and the empty biproduct $r=0$.

source.place: Lemma 9.33, printed p.176, second paragraph and footnote 7; explicit one-coordinate kernel inverse.

proof.text: The zero object with its zero vector is monogenic. Hence the set of dimensions of monogenic pairs is a nonempty subset of $\{0,\ldots,d^2\}$ by steps 3–4. Choose a largest attained value and a monogenic pair $(P,p)$ attaining it. In particular $\dim F(P)\leq d^2$. Essential smallness permits taking a skeleton when forming this set of attained dimensions; no maximum over a proper class is needed.

source.place: Printed p.176, paragraph between Lemmas 9.33 and 9.34.

proof.text: For $f,g:P\to Y$ with $F(f)p=F(g)p$, let $i:E\hookrightarrow P$ be the kernel of $f-g$. Since $F$ preserves this kernel by [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology], $p$ lifts to $F(E)$. Monogenicity of $(P,p)$ makes $i$ invertible. Then $(f-g)i=0$ implies $f=g$. Thus evaluation at $p$ is injective for every $Y$.

source.place: Lemma 9.34(a), printed p.176, uniqueness via the equalizer.

proof.text: For $y\in F(Y)$ let $i:Q\hookrightarrow P\oplus Y$ be the subobject generated by $(p,y)$ from [lem-sfb-fibre-generated-subobject], and let $q$ be its lifted generator. Put $u=\pi_Pi$ and $v=\pi_Yi$. Then $F(u)q=p$ and $F(v)q=y$. The image subobject of $u$ has fibre containing $p$, by image preservation [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology], so monogenicity of $P$ makes this image all of $P$. Hence $F(u)$ is onto. The pair $(Q,q)$ is monogenic by step 2, so maximality of $\dim F(P)$ gives $\dim F(Q)\leq\dim F(P)$. Surjectivity gives the reverse inequality; equal dimensions make $F(u)$ invertible. Step 1 makes $u$ invertible. Therefore $h=vu^{-1}:P\to Y$ satisfies $F(h)p=F(v)q=y$. This proves surjectivity for every $Y$, including $Y=0$.

source.place: Lemma 9.34(a), printed p.176, existence via the generated subobject of the product.

proof.text: Each evaluation map $\alpha_Y(h)=F(h)p$ is $k$-linear because $F$ is $k$-linear and evaluation of linear maps at a fixed vector is linear. By steps 6–7 it is bijective, so it is a linear isomorphism. For $a:Y\to Y'$ and $h:P\to Y$, functoriality gives $\alpha_{Y'}(ah)=F(a)F(h)p=F(a)\alpha_Y(h)$, proving naturality. The bound is step 5. If $X=0$ then $d=0$ and the chosen $P$ has zero fibre; every $Y$ has zero fibre as a subquotient of a zero sum, so the same maps are isomorphisms of zero spaces. Thus no nonzero-object assumption has entered.

source.place: Lemma 9.34(a), printed p.176; linearity, naturality and the permitted zero case made explicit.
